title: Company Fundamentals
promise: Charts show how a stock moves. Fundamentals tell you what the business is actually worth.
unlock: Know what you really own when you buy a share
Tell sales from profit, and read a margin
Work out EPS and the P/E, and what a high P/E expects
Check that profit turns into cash, and what debt does in a bad year
Read an earnings report in five minutes

questions.q: A company is split into 10,000,000 shares. You own 100,000 of them. What do you own?
options: A loan you get back with interest
questions.why: A share is a slice of ownership, not a loan. 100,000 slices out of 10,000,000 is one slice in every 100.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy · Feedback line written for the Academy (the board shows only Q2’s)

questions.q: Acme’s revenue grew from $80M to $100M. Profit stayed at $8M. What happened to its margin?
questions.why: Margin is profit ÷ revenue. The same profit on more sales means each dollar keeps less.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

questions.q: Northwind trades at $60 a share. Its EPS is $3. What is its P/E, and what does it mean?
options: 20: buyers pay $20 for each $1 of yearly profit
questions.why: P/E is price ÷ EPS: how many dollars buyers pay for $1 of yearly profit. It isn’t a verdict and it isn’t a margin.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy · Feedback line written for the Academy (the board shows only Q2’s)

questions.q: Both firms earn $10M before interest. Acme has no debt. Northwind pays $9M interest a year. Next year both earn only $5M before interest. Who is in trouble?
options: Acme: it has no loan to fall back on
Northwind: its interest is bigger than its earnings
questions.why: Interest costs the same in a bad year. Northwind’s $9M bill is bigger than its $5M of earnings. Acme keeps all of its $5M.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy · Feedback line written for the Academy (the board shows only Q2’s)

questions.q: Analysts expected EPS of $0.80. Acme reports $0.90, but cuts its guidance for next year. The price falls. Why?
options: The EPS beat was too small
The market weighs the future: the guidance cut
questions.why: EPS beat what was expected, but the price moves most on what’s next. A guidance cut says next year looks weaker.
questions.work: Reported $0.90 − expected $0.80 = a $0.10 beat. Guidance: cut.

retry.q: A company has 1,000 shares. You own 50 of them. What do you own?
options: A loan the company pays back
retry.why: A share is a slice of ownership, not a loan. 50 slices out of 1,000 is 5 in every 100.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy (the boards show only “Retry with new questions”)

retry.q: Northwind’s revenue fell from $200M to $160M. Profit stayed at $16M. What happened to its margin?
retry.why: Margin is profit ÷ revenue. The same profit on fewer sales means each dollar keeps more.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy (the boards show only “Retry with new questions”)

retry.q: Acme trades at $45 a share. Its EPS is $1.50. What is its P/E, and what does it mean?
options: 30: buyers pay $30 for each $1 of yearly profit
retry.why: P/E is price ÷ EPS: how many dollars buyers pay for $1 of yearly profit. It isn’t a verdict and it isn’t a margin.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy (the boards show only “Retry with new questions”)

retry.q: Northwind earns $12M before interest and pays $10M interest a year. Next year it earns only $7M before interest. What’s left?
retry.why: Interest costs the same in a bad year. $7M of earnings can’t cover a $10M interest bill.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy (the boards show only “Retry with new questions”)

retry.q: Northwind beats on revenue and on EPS, then cuts its sales forecast for next year. The price falls 7%. Which line moved it?
retry.why: Revenue and EPS both beat what was expected. The forecast cut was the bad surprise, and the market weighs the future most.

refresher.title: Lesson 1 · What a share really is
refresher.text: A share is a slice of ownership, not a loan. Your shares ÷ all the shares = your slice: 5 of 100 is 5%. Price × all the shares = the company’s market value.

refresher.title: Lesson 2 · Revenue, profit and margins
refresher.text: Margin = profit ÷ revenue. Sales can grow while each dollar keeps less. $8M profit on $100M of sales is an 8% margin, not 10%.

refresher.title: Lesson 3 · Earnings per share and the P/E
refresher.text: EPS = profit ÷ shares. P/E = price ÷ EPS: $50 ÷ $5 = 10, so buyers pay $10 for each $1 of yearly profit. A high P/E means high expectations.

refresher.title: Lesson 4 · Debt and cash flow
refresher.text: Interest costs the same in good and bad years. Earn $9M with $12M of interest to pay and you make a $3M loss. And check that profit turns into cash.

refresher.title: Lesson 5 · Reading an earnings report in 5 minutes
refresher.text: Check revenue and EPS against what was expected, then the guidance. Price reacts to surprises, and the outlook for next year often matters most.
